In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the UPGMA and the Bayesian approach are both consistent, whereas the ML and the NJ methods are both inconsistent.

the UPGMA method is statistically consistent in recovering the correct species tree from concatenated sequences generated from gene trees that are generated from a species tree in the anomaly zone (or even slightly outside the anomaly zone).

the ML method, with or without molecular clock assumption, is statistically inconsistent for estimating the topology and branch lengths of the true species tree, whereas other methods such as UPGMA, neighbor-joining (Saitou and Nei 1987), and BEST, are statistically consistent.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the ML estimate of a species tree for concatenated DNA sequence data is inconsistent when the gene trees are simulated from species trees within the anomaly zone, whereas a variety of other methods are consistent.
UPGMA is statistically consistent for recovering phylogenetic trees, and that ML is not.

the UPGMA and BEST methods, when applied to concatenated sequences simulated from species trees located in the anomaly zones, are statistically consistent, whereas the maximum likelihood method is inconsistent.
The main takeaway from our work is that
phylogenetic trees can be inferred from concatenated sequences generated from gene trees in the anomaly, even though the ML estimate is inconsistent.
methods that rely on relative divergence times to estimate phylogenies are statistically consistent, even when DNA sequences generated from gene trees in the anomaly-zone are analyzed.
phylogenetic trees estimated from concatenated sequences generated from species trees with short internal branches will be consistent with the true species tree.
